chapter_title: The Linux Terminal and Basic Commands
chapter_summary:
The terminal, also called the command line or shell, is a text-based interface for controlling the operating system. On Raspberry Pi OS, the default shell is called Bash. Many tasks that can be done by clicking icons on the desktop can also be done faster in the terminal. More importantly, the terminal is the only way to control a headless Raspberry Pi over SSH.

When you open a terminal, you see a prompt. It usually looks something like this:

```bash
alex@raspberrypi:~ $
```

This prompt tells you several things: the current user is `alex`, the hostname of the Pi is `raspberrypi`, the current directory is `~` which means the user's home folder, and the `$` indicates a normal user prompt. A `#` prompt would indicate the root user, who has full administrative power.

The Linux file system is organized as a tree. The top of the tree is called the root directory and is written as `/`. Inside `/` are folders such as `bin`, `etc`, `home`, `var`, and `usr`. User files live inside `/home/username`. When you open a terminal, you usually start in your home directory, written as `~`.

Here are the most important commands for beginners:

- `pwd` prints the current working directory.
- `ls` lists files and folders in the current directory. Use `ls -la` to show hidden files and detailed permissions.
- `cd` changes directory. `cd ..` goes up one level. `cd ~` goes to the home directory.
- `mkdir` creates a new directory. `mkdir projects` creates a folder called projects.
- `touch` creates an empty file. `touch notes.txt` creates a file called notes.txt.
- `cp` copies a file. `cp notes.txt backup.txt` makes a copy.
- `mv` moves or renames a file. `mv notes.txt old_notes.txt` renames it.
- `rm` removes a file. `rm notes.txt` deletes it. Use `rm -r foldername` to delete a directory and its contents.
- `clear` clears the terminal screen.
- `history` shows a list of previously typed commands.

Most commands accept options that change their behavior. Options usually start with a dash. For example, `ls -l` shows a long listing with file sizes and dates, and `ls -a` shows hidden files. Options can be combined: `ls -la` does both.

Tab completion is a huge time-saver. Start typing a file or command name and press the Tab key. The shell will complete the name if there is only one possibility, or show options if there are several. This reduces typing errors and speeds up navigation.

narration.text: Welcome. In this chapter you'll learn how to open and use the Raspberry Pi terminal, what the shell prompt tells you, and the basic file-management commands that let you move, copy, create, and remove files. The terminal is a compact, powerful way to control your Pi, and it becomes essential if you run the Pi without its desktop or connect over a network. We'll cover the commands you use most often, how options change their behavior, and two productivity features — tab completion and command history — that save time and reduce mistakes. For example, you will use the command that prints your current folder to confirm where you are, and the list command with options to reveal hidden files and permissions. Each lesson pairs a short terminal example with clear explanation and a small hands-on activity you can try on your Pi. By the end you will be able to create a practice folder, make and rename files, copy backups, and clean up safely. Notice common pitfalls like deleting the wrong file and the difference between regular and root prompts. Ready to begin exploring the shell with confidence and safety?

Specifically, you will be able to confirm your current folder, list files with details, navigate the filesystem, create and remove directories and files, move and copy items, and use helpful options that change command behavior. Each skill is paired with a short hands-on task so you practice safely. For example, after learning the list command with the long option you'll use it to reveal hidden configuration files in a directory. These objectives prepare you for both graphical and headless workflows on the Pi and make later scripting tasks much easier.

screens.title: What is the terminal and the shell?
screens.subtitle: Definitions, roles, and why Bash matters on Raspberry Pi OS

narration.text: The terminal is a text-based interface that accepts typed commands and shows text output. The shell is the program that interprets those commands; on Raspberry Pi OS the default shell is called Bash. Think of the terminal as the window that connects you to the shell process, and the shell as the conversational agent that understands your instructions. This model matters because some operations only make sense in a shell, like running scripts, piping outputs, and using command substitution. A concrete example: when you SSH into a headless Pi, you interact with Bash entirely through the terminal — there is no desktop. A common misconception is that the terminal itself does the work; it does not. The shell executes commands, talks to the kernel, and provides features like tab completion and history. Another confusion is between shell and terminal applications — you can use different shells inside the same terminal program. The core takeaway is to treat the terminal as your access point and Bash as the interpreter; learning basic shell features lets you automate tasks, recover systems, and work faster than relying only on graphical tools. How could you use a shell script to automate a repeated sequence you practice here?

keyIdea.title: Terminal vs shell
keyIdea.text: Terminal = interface window. Shell = command interpreter (Bash). Together they let you control a Pi textually and automate tasks.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Terminal & Shell
Definition and role
The terminal provides the interface; the shell interprets commands and communicates with the operating system kernel.
Concrete example
When you SSH into a Pi from another computer, you open a terminal and interact with Bash. There is no graphical desktop, so the shell is your control layer.
Common misconception
The terminal does not execute commands itself; it only displays input and output. The shell executes and provides features like completion and history.
Key takeaway
Learning shell features unlocks automation and headless administration on the Pi.
Analogy
Think of the terminal as a telephone and the shell as the person on the other end who follows your spoken instructions.
Example terminal snippet (visual only)
alex@raspberrypi:~ $  # prompt shows user, host, directory, and prompt symbol
Try this
Open a terminal on your Pi and notice the prompt. Say the user and folder out loud to build awareness before running commands.

screens.title: Reading the command prompt
screens.subtitle: What each part of the prompt tells you and why you should check it first

narration.text: A typical prompt on Raspberry Pi looks like the user's name, an at sign, the hostname, a colon, the current directory, and a symbol that shows your privilege level. For example, you might see the username followed by the device name and then the tilde to indicate the home directory, ending with a dollar sign for a normal user. Each element is meaningful: the user and hostname tell you who and where you are connected; the current directory tells you the folder that commands will act on; and the symbol at the end signals whether you have ordinary privileges or root privileges. Why check it first? Because running a destructive command in the wrong folder or as the root user can have serious consequences. A common mistake is assuming you are in your home folder when you are actually in a system folder. A quick habit: glance at the prompt, run the command that prints your current folder to confirm, and then continue. This small habit prevents the most frequent accidental deletions and misplaced files. Where could this habit save you in your own projects?

keyIdea.title: Prompt checklist
keyIdea.text: Always read user, hostname, current directory, and privilege symbol before running commands that change files or system state.

content.html:

Prompt anatomy
User, host, working directory, and privilege indicator form a short safety snapshot before you run commands.
Why it matters
Knowing where commands run prevents accidental damage and helps you target the correct files for copying or deletion.
Misconception
Seeing a dollar sign does not guarantee safety: you could still be in a system folder owned by your user account. Confirm the directory explicitly first.
Check
Habit: glance at prompt, run the current-directory command to confirm, then execute file changes.
Visual callout
Prompt example (visual only)

screens.title: Filesystem layout: root and home
screens.subtitle: How Linux arranges files and where user files live

narration.text: Linux organizes files in a hierarchical tree with a single root at the top, written as slash. Under that root you will find system folders like bin, etc, usr, var, and home. Your personal files live inside the home folder in a subdirectory named after your user. For example, if your username is alex, your files are under home slash alex. When a prompt shows a tilde, it means the current directory is your home folder. Understanding this layout helps you choose the right command targets and avoid system directories that require care. A common beginner error is creating files in the root folder because of a mistaken path — that often needs administrative privileges and can confuse system behavior. In practical terms, when you create a directory for practice, put it inside your home folder so you keep experiments isolated. The key takeaway: always know which branch of the filesystem tree you are on before manipulating files, and prefer working in your home directory for everyday tasks. Filesystem layout: root and home means root slash is the top. user files live under home. use the home directory for practice and system directories only when necessary.. In practical terms, how linux arranges files and where user files live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Filesystem tree
keyIdea.text: Root slash is the top. User files live under home. Use the home directory for practice and system directories only when necessary.

Tree structure
Root is written as slash. Home is where user folders live. System folders are separate branches that provide services and binaries.
Common folders
Examples include bin for essential programs, etc for configuration, usr for installed packages, var for variable data, and home for user files.
Tip
Keep practice folders in home. Avoid creating files directly under root or system directories unless you need administrative access.

screens.title: Confirm location and list files: pwd and ls
screens.subtitle: Print the working directory and list contents with useful options

narration.text: Two foundational commands let you confirm where you are and what is inside a directory. The first prints the current working directory so you never act in the wrong place. The second lists files and folders; with options it increases the detail you see. A practical sequence: first run the command that prints the current folder to verify you're in your home or practice directory. Then run the listing command with a long option to show file sizes, ownership, and dates. Add the option that reveals hidden files when you expect system or configuration files to be present. A typical combined form applies both options together so you see hidden files with full metadata. Use this habit before copying or deleting items. A common misconception is assuming list shows everything by default; hidden files begin with a dot and require the option to display them. The concrete example you will practice shows creating three files and then listing them with the detailed, show-hidden form so you can read permissions and confirm the files exist. Key takeaway: confirm your location and use listing options to avoid surprises.

keyIdea.title: Confirm & inspect
keyIdea.text: Use the print-directory command to confirm your location. Use list with options to inspect files before acting.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › pwd & ls
Commands to confirm and inspect
Check your working directory and use list options to reveal hidden files and detailed attributes.
Visual examples (type these in your terminal)
# prints the current directory
alex@raspberrypi:~ $ pwd
/home/alex

# list with details and hidden files
alex@raspberrypi:~ $ ls -la
total 20
drwxr-xr-x 4 alex alex 4096 Jun 1 10:00 .
# ...
Explanation & checklist
  • Always run the print-directory command before destructive actions to confirm context.
  • Use list with the long option to read permissions, sizes, and modification times.
  • When you expect configuration or hidden files, include the option to show hidden entries.
  • Combine options when you want both detail and hidden files in one view.
Key Takeaway
Confirm your location and inspect files with detail and hidden flags before changing anything.

screens.title: Change directory: cd and navigation shortcuts
screens.subtitle: Move around the filesystem quickly and predictably

narration.text: Changing directories is how you tell the shell which folder to operate in. The change-directory command accepts relative and absolute paths, and there are convenient shortcuts: two dots move up one level, and a tilde returns you to your home folder. These small shortcuts save many keystrokes and are essential for fast navigation. For example, if you are in home slash projects slash demo, running the two-dots shortcut moves you to home slash projects. If you want to return to your home folder regardless of where you are, using the tilde is immediate. A common beginner error is relying only on typing long paths; when paths are long, tab completion helps avoid mistakes. Another misconception is that moving up with two dots modifies files — it only changes your current location. Practice sequences: confirm your location, move into a new directory, move up with two dots, and return home with the tilde. Use these motions to reach the practice folder before creating files. The key skill is predicting the result of each navigation command before you press Enter. Change directory: cd and navigation shortcuts means use relative paths, two dots to go up, and tilde to return home. combine with tab completion for faster, safer moves.. In practical terms, move around the filesystem quickly and predictably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Navigation shortcuts
keyIdea.text: Use relative paths, two dots to go up, and tilde to return home. Combine with tab completion for faster, safer moves.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › cd & Navigation
Move through folders
Relative and absolute paths, parent and home shortcuts, and safe navigation practices.
Relative vs absolute
Relative paths are relative to your current directory. Absolute paths begin at root and always point to the same location.
Shortcuts
Two dots move up one level. Tilde returns you to your home directory. These are fast and predictable.
Example sequence
Example navigation (visual only)
alex@raspberrypi:~/projects/demo $ cd ..
alex@raspberrypi:~/projects $ cd ~
alex@raspberrypi:~ $
Try
Practice moving into your linux_practice folder, go up twice with two dots, then return home. Predict each new prompt before running the command.

screens.title: Create files and folders: mkdir and touch
screens.subtitle: Make directories and empty files for practice and organization

narration.text: Creating directories and files is one of the most common tasks in the shell. The make-directory command creates a folder when you need a new place to organize files. The touch command creates an empty file if it does not exist, or updates the file's modification time if it does. A practical practice: create a folder called linux practice inside your home folder, then use the create-file command to make three text files. Afterwards, list the directory contents with detail to confirm they exist. Why use empty files for practice? They are harmless placeholders that let you exercise copy, rename, and delete operations without risking important data. A common misconception is that touch writes content into a file — it does not; it only creates an empty entry. Another point: mkdir can create nested directories with an option so you don't need to create each parent manually. The concrete example here shows the commands you will type and the expected output, so you can run the sequence and confirm results visually. Key takeaway: use directories to isolate experiments, and use empty files as safe targets for file operations.

keyIdea.title: Create safely
keyIdea.text: Use directories to contain experiments and create empty files as safe placeholders before practicing copy or delete commands.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › mkdir & touch
Create directories and files
Use a folder for practice and create empty files to test copy and rename operations safely.
Example sequence (visual only)
alex@raspberrypi:~ $ mkdir linux_practice
alex@raspberrypi:~ $ cd linux_practice
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ touch file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ ls -la
Notes & tips
  • Use a single create-file command to make multiple empty files at once by listing names.
  • mdir can create nested folders when you include the option to create parents automatically.
  • Empty files are perfect test objects; they won't hold secrets and are easy to remove.
Key Takeaway
Create a dedicated practice folder in your home and populate it with empty files to learn safely.

screens.title: Copying and renaming: cp and mv
screens.subtitle: Create backups and rename files with confidence

narration.text: Copy and move are two related but different operations. The copy command makes an independent duplicate of a file, while the move command renames or relocates a file without creating a separate copy. Use copy when you want a backup before editing; use move when you want to rename or reorganize without keeping the original. A concrete example: after creating notes in a practice file, copy it to a backup file so you can experiment without losing the original content. If you only need to rename a file, move is the shorter, safer operation because it preserves the file's data under a new name. A common misconception is that move undoes changes; it does not — it only changes the file's name or folder reference. Also be careful when moving across filesystems, because move behaves like copy-then-delete in that case. Practice sequence: copy a file to notes_backup, then rename the original to notes_old with move. Verify both files exist with list. Key takeaway: use copy for backups and move for renames or relocations, and always verify results with a detailed listing.

keyIdea.title: Copy vs move
keyIdea.text: Use copy to keep backups, and move to rename or relocate. Verify both source and target exist after the operation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › cp & mv
Safely copy and rename
Copy creates a separate file. Move renames or relocates without keeping a separate copy unless you explicitly make one first.
Example sequence (visual only)
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ cp notes.txt notes_backup.txt
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ mv file1.txt notes_old.txt
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ ls -la
Practical notes
  • Make a copy before editing critical files to avoid accidental data loss.
  • Use move to rename files quickly; verify names with a listing afterwards.
  • When moving between devices, the shell may copy then delete; confirm both sides if necessary.
Key Takeaway
Always copy for backups and move for renames; verify with a detailed listing after each change.

screens.title: Deleting files: rm and safe practices
screens.subtitle: How removal works and how to avoid costly mistakes

narration.text: The remove command deletes files and, with an option, removes directories and their contents recursively. Because deletions can be irreversible from the shell, treat removal commands with great care. Always confirm the prompt and the current directory first, and prefer moving files to a temporary folder when you are unsure. A common beginner error is running a recursive removal with a broad pattern that deletes more than intended. You can mitigate risk by listing targets first, using precise names, and avoiding wildcard expansions until you test the pattern. Another safety pattern is to make a backup copy before removing important files. The concrete example you will practice shows listing the contents, moving a file to a safe backups folder, and then using remove to delete only the practice files. Also note that some shells and distributions offer an interactive option that asks for confirmation on each file; this adds friction but increases safety. Key takeaway: treat remove as irreversible and build confirmation habits to avoid accidental data loss. Deleting files: rm and safe practices means removal can be destructive. list targets, back up before deleting, and prefer precise names or interactive options to avoid mistakes.. In practical terms, how removal works and how to avoid costly mistakes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Remove with care
keyIdea.text: Removal can be destructive. List targets, back up before deleting, and prefer precise names or interactive options to avoid mistakes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › rm & Safety
Comparison: remove vs move backup
Removing deletes data. Moving to a backup folder preserves a copy you can restore.
Safer pattern
List files first, copy important files to a backup folder, then remove only the intended targets.
Common mistake
Using recursive removal with broad patterns can remove system or personal files unintentionally.
Example workflow
Visual only
# list and inspect
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ ls -la
# move to backup folder first
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ mv file1.txt ../backups/
# then remove only what you intend
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ rm file2.txt
Check your plan
Before removing, ask: Have I listed the files? Is there a backup? Am I in the expected directory?

screens.title: Command options and flags
screens.subtitle: How to change a command's behavior safely and combine options

narration.text: Many commands accept options, often called flags, that modify their behavior. Options usually start with a dash and can request additional detail, change output formatting, or make operations recursive. For example, a list command gains detail with the long option and shows hidden files with the show-hidden option; combined, you get both behaviors at once. The important idea is to read options carefully before using them and to try non-destructive options first, such as listing rather than deleting. A practical habit: when learning a new command, run it with an option that shows what it would do without changing anything. Options can usually be combined, which keeps typing concise but also requires you to understand their joint effect. A common mistake is assuming two options are independent; sometimes one option changes how another behaves. The concrete exercise here is to list files with combined options, then try the same options on a small sample to observe the difference. Key takeaway: use flags to tailor commands, but verify results on safe samples before applying them widely. Command options and flags means options change behavior and can be combined. test on safe examples first and prefer non-destructive flags during discovery.. In practical terms, how to change a command's behavior safely and combine options. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use options wisely
keyIdea.text: Options change behavior and can be combined. Test on safe examples first and prefer non-destructive flags during discovery.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Options & Flags
What options do
Options let you request more detail or change how a command behaves. Combine them thoughtfully and test first.
Combine options
You can pass multiple options together; for listing, combined options show both hidden entries and long details at once.
Test before change
When exploring an unfamiliar option that may modify files, try a read-only variant first to see the effect.
Example
Visual only
# combined options give more insight
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ ls -la
# -l shows details, -a shows hidden files
Key Takeaway
Combine flags to tune commands, but always test on safe examples first to confirm behavior.

screens.title: Tab completion and history
screens.subtitle: Speed up typing and recover previous commands

narration.text: Two productivity features make terminal use much faster: tab completion and the command history. Tab completion reduces typing and prevents typos by finishing filenames or command names when there is a single match or by offering choices when there are multiple matches. Use it to navigate long paths or to fill file names precisely. The command history remembers previously typed commands; you can browse, search, and rerun past commands instead of retyping them. A practical habit: type the first few letters of a prior command and use history search or repeat it with a quick keystroke. Together, these features reduce errors and save time during repetitive tasks. A common misconception is that history will automatically remember only successful commands; it records what you typed, so be careful about sensitive information. A concrete exercise: create files, use tab completion to fill names when copying, then use history to rerun a previous copy command and edit the destination. Key takeaway: combine tab completion and history to work faster and with fewer mistakes, but be mindful of what you store in history. Tab completion and history means use tab completion to avoid typos and history to rerun or refine prior commands. both save time and reduce errors.. In practical terms, speed up typing and recover previous commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Speed features
keyIdea.text: Use tab completion to avoid typos and history to rerun or refine prior commands. Both save time and reduce errors.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Tab Completion & History
Type less, do more
Tab completion completes names and shows choices. History lets you find and rerun previous commands.
Tab completion
Start typing a name and press Tab. If one match exists it completes; if many exist it lists options to choose from.
History
Use the history command or keyboard shortcuts to search and rerun earlier commands without retyping them.
Practice
Visual hints
# type 'no' then press Tab to complete 'notes.txt'
# use history to find recent copy commands
alex@raspberrypi:~/linux_practice $ history | grep cp
Key Takeaway
Learn a few keyboard shortcuts and use tab completion plus history to work with speed and accuracy.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What to remember from the terminal basics

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas. First, the terminal is the window and the shell is the interpreter; learning Bash gives you powerful control over the Pi. Second, always read the prompt: it tells you the user, hostname, current directory, and privilege level — this prevents many mistakes. Third, the filesystem is a tree with root at the top and your personal files in a home folder; keep practice work in home. These concepts are compact but foundational. You will rely on them repeatedly as you navigate, manage files, or work on headless systems. To reinforce these ideas, try naming out loud the prompt parts and point to your home folder in the prompt each time before running a command. That small habit builds situational awareness and prevents accidental system changes.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Terminal + shell, read the prompt, and work in your home directory for safe practice.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Key Concepts
Terminal & Shell
Terminal is the interface; the shell interprets commands. Together they enable scripting and headless access.
Read the Prompt
User, host, directory, privilege symbol — check them to avoid surprises before running commands.
Home vs Root
Use your home directory for practice; avoid system directories unless you have a specific reason and permissions.
Quick takeaway
Build habits: check the prompt, confirm the working directory, and keep experiments in home.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Essential commands and productivity tips to keep practicing

narration.text: Finally, remember the core commands and the habits that make them safe and efficient. The print-directory command confirms where you are. The list command, especially combined with options, shows hidden files and permissions. Change-directory moves you through folders using shortcuts like parent and home. Use make-directory and create-file to prepare practice spaces, and copy and move to back up or rename files. Treat remove as destructive and back up before you delete. For speed, learn tab completion and use the history to rerun or refine earlier commands. A simple assessment: when asked to list all files including hidden ones with details, you will run the list command with the appropriate options. Practice the guided lab sequence and check your prompt at each step; that combination of commands and habits is what makes you a confident terminal user.

keyIdea.title: Commands & habits
keyIdea.text: Master print-directory, list, change-directory, make-directory, touch, copy, move, remove, and use options, tab completion, and history to work safely.

Productivity
